explanations.explanation: Cherubim, skillfully worked right into the linen. God says it again for the veil, "…with cherubim skillfully worked into it." (Exodus 26:31). Those curtains and that veil were works of art, and I'm over here proud when my stamp comes out straight.

I like the energy, friend, because lions are a bold choice. But the text says nothing about lions in the linen. God says the curtains get blue, purple and scarlet yarn, with cherubim skillfully worked into them. Save the lions for another day.

Pomegranates are a nice thought, but they aren't in this passage's curtains. What God says to work into the ten linen curtains is cherubim. Blue, purple and scarlet yarn is the color, and the cherubim are the design.

explanations.answer: So the tabernacle is one unit
explanations.explanation: That's the reason God gives. The fifty gold clasps join the two sets of curtains "…so that the tabernacle will be a unit." Two sets of five go in, and one tabernacle comes out. That's the kind of teamwork I like to see.

explanations.answer: So the light can shine through
explanations.explanation: I can see why you'd think that, friend, but the text never mentions light shining through anything here. God gives a different reason for the fifty gold clasps. He says they join the curtains together "…so that the tabernacle will be a unit."

explanations.answer: So each set can stand alone
explanations.explanation: That's a fair thought, friend, but the text goes another way. The fifty gold clasps join the two sets of five curtains, and God gives the reason: "…so that the tabernacle will be a unit." (Exodus 26:6). Two sets go in and one tabernacle comes out.

I get it, friend. Most of us would grab the scissors and tidy things up. But God says the opposite. The leftover half curtain hangs down over the back of the tabernacle, and the extra cubit on each side hangs over the sides to cover it (Exodus 26:12-13). Nothing gets trimmed.

Right, nothing gets trimmed. The half curtain left over "…shall hang down over the back of the tabernacle." And the tent curtains will be a cubit longer on either side, with the excess hanging over the sides to cover it (Exodus 26:12-13). The extra is part of the plan, and I wish my cookie crumbs were treated that well.

Pattern is the word. God says to set up the tabernacle "…according to the pattern shown you on the mountain." Moses isn't making it up as he goes. He was shown it, and that's more than I get with half my recipes.

A promise is a good thing, friend, but that's not the word here. God says the tabernacle is set up "…according to the pattern shown you on the mountain." Moses has something to follow, because he was shown it.
No warning in this verse, friend. It's calmer than that. God says to set up the tabernacle "…according to the pattern shown you on the mountain." Moses was shown a pattern to follow.

Yes! God says to "…place the ark of the Testimony behind the veil." The veil then separates the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place (Exodus 26:33). The ark gets the room behind the veil, and the mercy seat goes on top of it (Exodus 26:34).

Close, but the lampstand doesn't go back there. God says to place the lampstand outside the veil, on the south side (Exodus 26:35). What goes behind the veil is the ark of the Testimony (Exodus 26:33).
Nope, friend, the table stays out front. God says to place it "…outside the veil on the north side of the tabernacle…" (Exodus 26:35). Behind the veil goes the ark of the Testimony (Exodus 26:33).

That's the one. God says the veil "…will separate the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place." (Exodus 26:33). The ark sits back there, and the mercy seat goes on top of it (Exodus 26:34). The name tells you something, friend.
Good guess, but that name isn't in this passage. The courtyard comes later, and it's out around the tabernacle. The text calls the room behind the veil "…the Most Holy Place." (Exodus 26:33).

That name isn't in this passage, friend. The Bible does mention an upper room in Acts 1:13, but it has nothing to do with this tent. Here, God says the veil separates the Holy Place from "…the Most Holy Place." (Exodus 26:33).

True! God says, "Put the mercy seat on the ark of the Testimony in the Most Holy Place." (Exodus 26:34). The ark sits behind the veil, and the mercy seat goes right on top of it. That's a good, clear instruction.

That one was True, friend. God says, "Put the mercy seat on the ark of the Testimony in the Most Holy Place." (Exodus 26:34). It goes on top of the ark, back there behind the veil. Easy one to second-guess, though.

explanations.answer: Outside the veil across from each other
explanations.explanation: You got it. God says to place the table outside the veil on the north side, and the lampstand opposite it on the south side (Exodus 26:35). Both stay outside the veil, facing each other across the room. I'd call that a very organized room.

explanations.answer: Behind the veil on each side of the ark
explanations.explanation: God does say to place the ark of the Testimony behind the veil, with the mercy seat on top (Exodus 26:33-34). But the table and the lampstand don't go back there. The instruction puts them outside the veil, the table on the north side and the lampstand opposite it on the south (Exodus 26:35).

explanations.answer: Side by side next to the entrance
explanations.explanation: Not side by side, friend. God puts them across from each other. The table goes outside the veil on the north side, and the lampstand goes opposite it on the south side (Exodus 26:35). It's one wall each, with the whole room between them.

I can see why you'd say that, friend, because silver bases are all over this chapter. But the five entrance posts get something different. God says to "…cast five bronze bases for them." (Exodus 26:37). The wall frames and the veil posts get the silver ones.

False is right. The posts are overlaid with gold and use gold hooks, but God says to "…cast five bronze bases for them." (Exodus 26:37). The wall frames stand on silver bases (Exodus 26:19). Same tent, different metal at the bottom.

A horn on each of the four corners. God says to make them "…so that the horns are of one piece…" so they're part of the altar and not stuck on afterward. The whole altar then gets overlaid with bronze.

I do love a bell, friend. Ruby, one of my cookie cutter kids, is one, and I remember how you could hear her from across the kitchen. But the altar doesn't get bells. God says to make a horn on each of its four corners, all one piece with the altar.

Cherubim do show up in this passage, but on the linen curtains and the veil (Exodus 26:1, 31). The altar gets something else. God says to make a horn on each of its four corners, all one piece with it.

Bronze it is, baker! The altar is overlaid with bronze, and the instruction says, "Make all its utensils of bronze…" (Exodus 27:3). Then the grate is bronze mesh with bronze rings (Exodus 27:4), the poles are overlaid with bronze (Exodus 27:6), and even the tent pegs are bronze (Exodus 27:19). Pots, shovels, bowls, forks, firepans, all one metal, a perfectly matching set. My spoons have never matched once, and I've stopped asking why.
Gold shows up in this passage, friend, but not on the altar. The frames, the crossbars and the veil posts get gold (Exodus 26:29, 32). The altar and all its utensils are bronze.

Silver is in there, but not here. It's on the bases under the wall frames, and on the hooks and bands of the courtyard posts (Exodus 26:19; 27:17). The altar is overlaid with bronze, and its utensils are made of bronze (Exodus 27:2-3).

explanations.answer: So the altar can be carried
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says. The poles "…are to be inserted into the rings so that the poles are on two sides of the altar when it is carried." Slide the poles in and it's ready to travel. I could use poles like that for my cookie trays.

explanations.answer: So the grate can be lifted out
explanations.explanation: I can see the thinking, friend. The grate does have a bronze ring at each corner (Exodus 27:4). But the text says what the poles are for. They go in the rings "…so that the poles are on two sides of the altar when it is carried."

explanations.answer: So the altar can be tied down
explanations.explanation: Tied down is almost the opposite, friend. The text says the poles go into the rings "…so that the poles are on two sides of the altar when it is carried." It's made to be carried.
Solid would be heavy, friend, but that's not what God says. He says, "Construct the altar with boards so that it is hollow." It's made of acacia wood, overlaid with bronze, and hollow on the inside.

False, and you read that right. God says, "Construct the altar with boards so that it is hollow." He adds that it is "…to be made just as you were shown on the mountain." Hollow it is, and I bet it carries easier too.

Right. The east side is fifty cubits wide, with fifteen cubits of curtain on each end. In between, "The gate of the courtyard shall be twenty cubits long…" (Exodus 27:14-16). Fifteen and fifteen and twenty makes fifty, so the math works out.

The altar is a good guess, but this passage doesn't place it on the east wall. What fills the middle of the east side is the gate of the courtyard, twenty cubits long (Exodus 27:16). Fifteen plus twenty plus fifteen makes fifty.

Easy to mix up, friend, because both have an embroidered curtain. But the tent's entrance is a different curtain, and it belongs to the tabernacle itself (Exodus 26:36). The east side of the courtyard has "The gate of the courtyard…" twenty cubits long (Exodus 27:16).

Plain would be easier to make, but that's not what God says. The gate gets "…a curtain embroidered with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and finely spun linen." (Exodus 27:16). The walls on either side are linen, and the gate is the colorful part.

False, and you caught it. God says the gate has "…a curtain embroidered with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and finely spun linen." (Exodus 27:16). It's the same blue, purple and scarlet the tabernacle curtains have. That gate shows up in color.

All the time is right, baker. The oil of pressed olives is for the light, and the lamps are to keep burning continually (Exodus 27:20). Then Aaron and his sons are to tend them "…from evening until morning." (Exodus 27:21). Evening until morning! I fall asleep waiting for one batch to cool, so I'd be the worst lamp crew in the camp.
Feast days aren't mentioned here, friend. God says the oil is "…to keep the lamps burning continually." (Exodus 27:20). It isn't saved for special days.
The Sabbath isn't mentioned in this part, friend. The instruction is bigger than one day. God says the oil is "…to keep the lamps burning continually." (Exodus 27:20).
That's right. God says, "…Aaron and his sons are to tend the lamps before the LORD…" (Exodus 27:21). Aaron is Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14). So the lamp job stays in the family.

I see why you'd pick Moses, since he's the one God is talking to. But the text names someone else for lamp duty. God says, "…Aaron and his sons are to tend the lamps before the LORD…" (Exodus 27:21). Aaron is Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14).

The elders aren't given this job, friend. God says, "…Aaron and his sons are to tend the lamps before the LORD…" (Exodus 27:21). Aaron is Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14), and he and his sons get the assignment.

True! Aaron and his sons are to tend the lamps "…from evening until morning." They do it in the Tent of Meeting, outside the veil, before the LORD (Exodus 27:21). That's the whole night shift, and I wouldn't trade my days for it.
That was True, friend. God says Aaron and his sons "…are to tend the lamps before the LORD from evening until morning." (Exodus 27:21). They do it in the Tent of Meeting, outside the veil.

I get why you'd think that, but the verse reaches further. God says, "This is to be a permanent statute for the Israelites for the generations to come." (Exodus 27:21). It doesn't stop at the wilderness. The lamps are meant for the long haul.

Right, friend, it isn't just for the wilderness. God says, "This is to be a permanent statute for the Israelites for the generations to come." (Exodus 27:21). Permanent, plus generations to come, means this one is meant to last.
